claim: GGGGCC microsatellite repeat RNA localizes to neuritic granules in iPSNs derived from C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion carriers.
source: We confirmed that iPSNs contained nuclear GGGGCC RNA foci, but also found that 78 ± 12% SD (carrier 1; n=25 neurons) and 75 ± 11% SD (carrier 2; n=23) of iPSNs that contained nuclear GGGGCC RNA foci also contained neuritic GGGGCC RNA particles by in situ hybridization (Figure 1A,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization experiments in iPSNs, with quantitative measurements and reference to Figure 1A,L.

claim: GGGGCC repeat RNA particles are detected both proximally and distally at over 45 μm from the cell body in neurites.
source: The GGGGCC RNA particles were detected both proximally and distally at over 45 μm from the cell body in neurites and were, in some cases, lined up, consistent with possible association with a cytoskeletal track (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from in situ hybridization with specific distance measurements and reference to Figure 1A-B.

claim: GGGGCC repeat RNA particles are sometimes lined up in neurites, consistent with possible association with a cytoskeletal track.
source: The GGGGCC RNA particles were detected both proximally and distally at over 45 μm from the cell body in neurites and were, in some cases, lined up, consistent with possible association with a cytoskeletal track (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed linear arrangement of RNA particles in neurites, suggesting association with cytoskeletal tracks.

claim: GGGGCC repeat RNA particles are detected in the cell body in nearly all iPSNs that also contained GGGGCC RNA nuclear foci.
source: In addition, GGGGCC repeat RNA particles were detected in the cell body in nearly all iPSNs that also contained GGGGCC RNA nuclear foci (Figure 1C, also Almeida et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from in situ hybridization and references both current data (Figure 1C) and a previous publication (Almeida et al., 2013).

claim: GGGGCC RNA was not detected in control iPSNs.
source: We did not detect GGGGCC RNA in control iPSNs, indicating that the non-expanded repeat is either present below the detection level or not stably expressed in wild-type iPSNs.
evidence: The claim is supported by negative experimental results from in situ hybridization in control iPSNs.

claim: The non-expanded GGGGCC repeat is either present below the detection level or not stably expressed in wild-type iPSNs.
source: We did not detect GGGGCC RNA in control iPSNs, indicating that the non-expanded repeat is either present below the detection level or not stably expressed in wild-type iPSNs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the negative detection results in control iPSNs.

claim: Expanded CAG repeat RNA localizes to discrete particles in neurites and in the cell body of primary rat spinal cord neurons.
source: As with the GGGGCC microsatellite repeat, we detected the expanded CAG repeat RNA in discrete particles in neurites, and in the cell body (Figure 1D–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization in primary rat spinal cord neurons expressing (CAG)100, with reference to Figure 1D-E and supplementary figures.

claim: Expanded CAG repeat RNA forms nuclear foci.
source: We also noted nuclear foci as previously described (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and references to previous descriptions of this phenomenon.

claim: Expanded CAG repeat RNA assumes stem-loop secondary structure.
source: Expanded CAG repeat RNA assumes stem-loop secondary structure (Michlewski and Krzyzosiak, 2004), confers neurodegeneration (Li et al., 2008), and has been noted to assemble into nuclear foci (Ho et al., 2005; Li et al., 2008; Wojciechowska and Krzyzosiak, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Michlewski and Krzyzosiak, 2004).

claim: Expanded CAG repeat RNA confers neurodegeneration.
source: Expanded CAG repeat RNA assumes stem-loop secondary structure (Michlewski and Krzyzosiak, 2004), confers neurodegeneration (Li et al., 2008), and has been noted to assemble into nuclear foci (Ho et al., 2005; Li et al., 2008; Wojciechowska and Krzyzosiak, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Li et al., 2008).

claim: MS2 RNA alone does not show enrichment in cellular processes.
source: Co-expression of NLS-CP-GFP with either of two control RNAs, the MS2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or LacZ-MS2 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) RNAs, produced results similar to NLS-CP-GFP alone: there was no enrichment of signal in cellular processes (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A for construct details).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from MS2 system experiments in primary rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: LacZ-MS2 RNA does not show enrichment in cellular processes.
source: Co-expression of NLS-CP-GFP with either of two control RNAs, the MS2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) or LacZ-MS2 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) RNAs, produced results similar to NLS-CP-GFP alone: there was no enrichment of signal in cellular processes (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A for construct details).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from MS2 system experiments in primary rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 1F and supplementary figures.

claim: GAA repeat RNA does not assume stem-loop secondary structure.
source: We then examined the localization of an expanded repeat RNA that does not assume stem-loop secondary structure, the GAA repeat associated with Friedreich's ataxia (Sobczak et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Sobczak et al., 2003).

claim: (GAA)100-MS2 RNA is not localized to neurites.
source: (GAA)100-MS2 did not alter the distribution of the GFP reporter, indicating this repeat RNA without secondary structure was not localized to neurites (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from MS2 system experiments showing no neuritic localization of (GAA)100-MS2, with reference to Figure 1G and supplementary figures.

claim: RNA particles were neuritic in <0.5% of neurons in cultures expressing NLS-CP-GFP with control LacZ-MS2 or (GAA)100-MS2 RNA.
source: RNA particles were neuritic in <0.5% of neurons in cultures expressing NLS-CP-GFP with control LacZ-MS2 or (GAA)100-MS2 RNA (Figure 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from MS2 system experiments, with reference to Figure 1M.

claim: 94.4 ± 9.6% SD of neurons cotransfected with NLS-CP-GFP and (CAG)100-MS2 contained particles in neurites.
source: In contrast, neurons transfected with NLS-CP-GFP and (CAG)100-MS2 had an RNA distribution like that of (CAG)100 by in situ hybridization (compare Figure 1H with 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H with Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), with 94.4 ± 9.6% SD (n=3 cultures, 87 neurons total) of cotransfected neurons containing particles in neurites (Figure 1M).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from MS2 system experiments in primary rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 1M.

claim: (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA is neuritically localized in 21.1 ± 3.7% SD of all neuron types in mixed spinal cord cultures.
source: Next, we examined (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA and found it neuritically localized in 21.1 ± 3.7% SD (n=4 cultures, 147 neurons total) of all neuron types in the cultures (Figures 1I,M, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), and in 66.6 ± 33.3% SD (n=3 cultures, 9 neurons total) of large neurons with a morphology characteristic of motor neurons (Figure 1M, at right; also Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from MS2 system experiments, with reference to Figures 1I, 1M, and supplementary figures.

claim: (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA is neuritically localized in 66.6 ± 33.3% SD of large neurons with a morphology characteristic of motor neurons.
source: Next, we examined (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA and found it neuritically localized in 21.1 ± 3.7% SD (n=4 cultures, 147 neurons total) of all neuron types in the cultures (Figures 1I,M, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), and in 66.6 ± 33.3% SD (n=3 cultures, 9 neurons total) of large neurons with a morphology characteristic of motor neurons (Figure 1M, at right; also Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from MS2 system experiments in motor neurons, with reference to Figure 1M and supplementary figures.

claim: CUG repeat RNA is highly structured and assumes stem-loop conformation.
source: The RNA repeat expansions associated with myotonic dystrophy types I and II—CUG and CCUG, respectively—are also highly structured RNAs that assume stem-loop conformation (Napierala and Krzyzosiak, 1997; Sobczak et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Napierala and Krzyzosiak, 1997; Sobczak et al., 2003).

claim: CCUG repeat RNA is highly structured and assumes stem-loop conformation.
source: The RNA repeat expansions associated with myotonic dystrophy types I and II—CUG and CCUG, respectively—are also highly structured RNAs that assume stem-loop conformation (Napierala and Krzyzosiak, 1997; Sobczak et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Napierala and Krzyzosiak, 1997; Sobczak et al., 2003).

claim: (CUG)100-MS2 RNA particles are present in neurites in over 75% of transfected neurons.
source: Indeed, (CUG)100-MS2 and (CCUG)100-MS2 RNA particles were also present in neurites in over 75% of the transfected neurons (Figure 1J-K,M, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from MS2 system experiments, with reference to Figure 1J-K, M and supplementary figures.

claim: (CCUG)100-MS2 RNA particles are present in neurites in over 75% of transfected neurons.
source: Indeed, (CUG)100-MS2 and (CCUG)100-MS2 RNA particles were also present in neurites in over 75% of the transfected neurons (Figure 1J-K,M, see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from MS2 system experiments, with reference to Figure 1J-K, M and supplementary figures.

claim: Disease severity and age of onset in patients with trinucleotide repeat expansion disorders correlates with increasing repeat number.
source: Disease severity and age of onset in patients with trinucleotide repeat expansion disorders (e.g. CAG and CUG) correlates with increasing repeat number (Orr and Zoghbi, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Orr and Zoghbi, 2007).

claim: The prevalence of neuritic CAG repeat RNA particles is highly correlated with increasing repeat number.
source: The fraction of primary arbors that had particles containing RNAs of 20, 40, 70, and 100 CAG repeats were 0.08 ± 0.07 SD, 0.20 ± 0.06 SD, 0.45 ± 0.07 SD, and 0.86 ± 0.10 SD, respectively (Figure 2A–D). These data indicate that, for CAG repeat RNA, there is repeat length specificity for neuritic localization as the prevalence of neuritic particles was highly correlated with increasing repeat number.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data showing increasing prevalence of neuritic particles with increasing CAG repeat length, with reference to Figure 2A-D.

claim: Three GGGGCC units are sufficient to confer neuritic localization.
source: These data indicate that three GGGGCC units, at the low end of non-expanded C9orf72 alleles (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Gijselinck et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2011; van der Zee et al., 2013), are sufficient to confer neuritic localization, and that targeting information is retained in expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing neuritic localization of (GGGGCC)3-MS2 and citations to previous publications defining the range of non-expanded alleles.

claim: Targeting information is retained in expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA.
source: These data indicate that three GGGGCC units, at the low end of non-expanded C9orf72 alleles (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Gijselinck et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2011; van der Zee et al., 2013), are sufficient to confer neuritic localization, and that targeting information is retained in expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that both (GGGGCC)3 and (GGGGCC)48 show neuritic localization.

claim: The fraction of primary arbors with (GGGGCC)3-MS2 RNA particles (0.69 ± 0.12 SD) is higher than the fraction with (GGGGCC)48-MS2 particles (0.24 ± 0.04 SD).
source: In contrast, the fraction of primary arbors with (GGGGCC)3-MS2 RNA particles (Figure 2E) was higher (0.69 ± 0.12 SD) than the fraction with (GGGGCC)48-MS2 particles (0.24 ± 0.04 SD) (Figure 2D), and the percentage of neurons in the mixed culture with neuritic particles was also higher for (GGGGCC)3-MS2 (46.4 ± 22.7% SD [n=3 cultures, 110 neurons total]), than for (GGGGCC)48-MS2 (21.1 ± 3.7% s.d. (n=4 cultures, 147 neurons total).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data comparing (GGGGCC)3-MS2 and (GGGGCC)48-MS2, with reference to Figure 2D-E.

claim: The percentage of neurons with neuritic particles is higher for (GGGGCC)3-MS2 (46.4 ± 22.7% SD) than for (GGGGCC)48-MS2 (21.1 ± 3.7% SD).
source: In contrast, the fraction of primary arbors with (GGGGCC)3-MS2 RNA particles (Figure 2E) was higher (0.69 ± 0.12 SD) than the fraction with (GGGGCC)48-MS2 particles (0.24 ± 0.04 SD) (Figure 2D), and the percentage of neurons in the mixed culture with neuritic particles was also higher for (GGGGCC)3-MS2 (46.4 ± 22.7% SD [n=3 cultures, 110 neurons total]), than for (GGGGCC)48-MS2 (21.1 ± 3.7% s.d. (n=4 cultures, 147 neurons total).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data comparing (GGGGCC)3-MS2 and (GGGGCC)48-MS2.

claim: Expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA may be less efficiently incorporated into RNA granules, or arbors with expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA may have degenerated.
source: These data may also suggest that expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA is less efficiently incorporated into RNA granules, or that arbors with expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA had degenerated (hence a lower fraction of arbors with particles).
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering possible explanations for the observed lower fraction of arbors with (GGGGCC)48-MS2 particles compared to (GGGGCC)3-MS2.

claim: (GGGGCC)48-MS2 particles undergo anterograde, retrograde, and bidirectional movement along neurites.
source: This approach showed that both (GGGGCC)48-MS2 and (CAG)100-MS2 particles were undergoing anterograde, retrograde, and bidirectional movement, both proximally as well as distally along neurites (Figure 3A–B, Videos 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-lapse imaging showing particle movement, with reference to Figure 3A-B and Videos 1-3.

claim: (CAG)100-MS2 particles undergo anterograde, retrograde, and bidirectional movement along neurites.
source: This approach showed that both (GGGGCC)48-MS2 and (CAG)100-MS2 particles were undergoing anterograde, retrograde, and bidirectional movement, both proximally as well as distally along neurites (Figure 3A–B, Videos 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-lapse imaging showing particle movement, with reference to Figure 3A-B and Videos 1-3.

claim: The mean average velocity of uninterrupted unidirectional movement is 1.06 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2.
source: Similar to previous reports for transport ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) and consistent with velocities for dynein or kinesin-mediated transport (Kiebler and Bassell, 2006), the mean average velocity of uninterrupted unidirectional movement was 1.06 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2, and 1.30 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2, and the average max velocity was 1.40 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2, and 1.85 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from time-lapse imaging analysis, with reference to Table 1 and citation to previous work on transport RNPs.

claim: The mean average velocity of uninterrupted unidirectional movement is 1.30 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2.
source: Similar to previous reports for transport ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) and consistent with velocities for dynein or kinesin-mediated transport (Kiebler and Bassell, 2006), the mean average velocity of uninterrupted unidirectional movement was 1.06 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2, and 1.30 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2, and the average max velocity was 1.40 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2, and 1.85 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from time-lapse imaging analysis, with reference to Table 1 and citation to previous work on transport RNPs.

claim: The average max velocity is 1.40 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2.
source: Similar to previous reports for transport ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) and consistent with velocities for dynein or kinesin-mediated transport (Kiebler and Bassell, 2006), the mean average velocity of uninterrupted unidirectional movement was 1.06 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2, and 1.30 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2, and the average max velocity was 1.40 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2, and 1.85 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from time-lapse imaging analysis, with reference to Table 1 and citation to previous work on transport RNPs.

claim: The average max velocity is 1.85 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2.
source: Similar to previous reports for transport ribonucleoprotein particles (RNPs) and consistent with velocities for dynein or kinesin-mediated transport (Kiebler and Bassell, 2006), the mean average velocity of uninterrupted unidirectional movement was 1.06 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2, and 1.30 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2, and the average max velocity was 1.40 μm/s for (GGGGCC)48-MS2, and 1.85 μm/s for (CAG)100-MS2 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from time-lapse imaging analysis, with reference to Table 1 and citation to previous work on transport RNPs.

claim: Particles that underwent corralled movements have a mean average basal velocity of 0.12 μm/s.
source: By contrast, particles that underwent corralled movements had a mean average basal velocity of 0.12 μm/s (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from time-lapse imaging analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Motile particles above background could not be detected in neurons expressing control RNAs LacZ-MS2 or MS2.
source: We could not detect motile particles above background in neurons expressing control RNAs LacZ-MS2 or MS2.
evidence: The claim is supported by negative experimental results from time-lapse imaging of control RNA-expressing neurons.

claim: Microsatellite repeat RNAs assemble into mRNA transport granules that are dynamic along neuronal projections.
source: These data indicate that the microsatellite repeat RNAs could be assembling into mRNA transport granules that are dynamic along the neuronal projections.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed movement of repeat RNA particles along neurites with velocities consistent with transport granules.

claim: Neurons with neuritically localized (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA have fewer primary branches (3.8 ± 1.6 SD; n=12 neurons) than neurons with nuclear (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA foci (6.2 ± 1.3 SD; n=12 neurons).
source: Neurons with neuritically localized (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA had, on average, fewer primary branches (3.8 ± 1.6 SD; n=12 neurons) than neurons with nuclear (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA foci (6.2 ± 1.3 SD; n=12 neurons), or than neurons with somatic but without neuritic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA (6.1 ± 2.1 SD; n=20 neurons) (compare Figure 3F with 3D and E, see Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from morphological analysis of transfected rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 3F, 3D, 3E, and 3H.

claim: Neurons with neuritically localized (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA have fewer primary branches than neurons with somatic but without neuritic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA (6.1 ± 2.1 SD; n=20 neurons).
source: Neurons with neuritically localized (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA had, on average, fewer primary branches (3.8 ± 1.6 SD; n=12 neurons) than neurons with nuclear (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA foci (6.2 ± 1.3 SD; n=12 neurons), or than neurons with somatic but without neuritic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA (6.1 ± 2.1 SD; n=20 neurons) (compare Figure 3F with 3D and E, see Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from morphological analysis of transfected rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 3F, 3D, 3E, and 3H.

claim: Neurons with neuritically localized (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA have fewer primary branches than neurons expressing the (GAA)100-MS2 control (8.4 ± 2.2 SD; n=21 neurons).
source: They also had fewer primary branches than neurons expressing the (GAA)100-MS2 control (8.4 ± 2.2 SD; n=21 neurons), which lacked neuritic RNA particles (compare Figure 3F with 3C, see Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from morphological analysis of transfected rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 3F, 3C, and 3H.

claim: Neurons with neuritically localized non-expanded (GGGGCC)3-MS2 RNA do not show dramatic primary branch loss.
source: In contrast, neurons with neuritically localized non-expanded (GGGGCC)3-MS2 RNA did not show a dramatic primary branch loss Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from morphological analysis of transfected rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 3G.

claim: Neurons with neuritically localized (GGGGCC)3-MS2 RNA have a similar average number of primary branches (6.4 ± 1.3 SD; n=20 neurons) compared with neurons with nuclear (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA foci or neurons with somatic but not neuritic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA.
source: These neurons had a similar average number of primary branches (6.4 ± 1.3 SD; n=20 neurons) compared with neurons with nuclear (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA foci, or neurons with somatic but not neuritic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA (Figure 3H, compare Figure 3G with 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from morphological analysis of transfected rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 3H, 3G, 3D, and 3E.

claim: There is no significant correlation between the presence of neuritic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA particles and expression level of the RNA in the soma.
source: We did not find a significant correlation between the presence of neuritic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA particles and expression level of the RNA in the soma (Figure 3I, average normalized mean intensity 0.56 ± 0.23 SD and 0.42 ± 0.25 SD; n=18 and 24 neurons total with neuritic or somatic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from expression level analysis, with reference to Figure 3I.

claim: The expression level of the RNA in the soma does not affect primary branch number.
source: Similarly, the expression level of the RNA in the soma did not affect primary branch number (Figure 3J; n = 76 neurons total).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from expression level and morphological analysis, with reference to Figure 3J.

claim: When (GGGGCC)48-MS2 repeat RNA is present in neuritic particles, there is a dramatic reduction in primary neural branches.
source: These data show that when the (GGGGCC)48-MS2 repeat RNA is present in neuritic particles, there is a dramatic reduction in primary neural branches—this is not the case when the RNA is nuclear or somatic.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on the experimental data comparing branching in neurons with neuritic, nuclear, or somatic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA.

claim: High expression is not required to drive (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA association into neuritic particles or to induce branching defects.
source: Furthermore, high expression is not required to drive (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA association into neuritic particles or to induce branching defects.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of correlation between expression level and neuritic localization or branching defects.

claim: The presence of (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA in neuritic particles is associated with deleterious effects on neuronal branching.
source: These data argue that the presence of the (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA in neuritic particles is associated with deleterious effects on neuronal branching.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed correlation between neuritic (GGGGCC)48-MS2 RNA and reduced branching.

claim: RAN translated peptide repeat proteins could not be detected using FLAG, HA and Myc tags in the experimental system.
source: Expanded repeat RNAs have also been reported to undergo translation into peptide repeat proteins. We looked for RAN translated peptide repeat proteins derived from the repeat RNAs (Ash et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2013; Zu et al., 2011) by immunostain utilizing FLAG, HA and Myc tags encoded 3' of the repeat in the three different reading frames, but were unable to provide evidence for the presence of RAN peptides with these constructs in this system (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Materials and methods for construct details).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative experimental results from immunostaining experiments, with citations to previous work on RAN translation.

claim: Branching defects in the experimental system may be mediated by neuritically localized expanded repeat RNA.
source: Because we observe a dramatic reduction of primary branches only in neurons with neuritic RNA granules, branching defects in our system may be mediated by neuritically localized expanded repeat RNA.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation between neuritic RNA localization and branching defects, and the absence of detectable RAN peptides.

claim: The toxicity conferred by the expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA is not simply due to neuritic granule association.
source: Moreover, our data suggest that the toxicity conferred by the expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA is not simply due to neuritic granule association, given that neuritically localized non-expanded (GGGGCC)3-MS2 RNA did not confer dramatic primary branch loss.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison between expanded (GGGGCC)48-MS2 and non-expanded (GGGGCC)3-MS2 effects on branching.

claim: Expression of UAS-(GGGGCC)48 results in dramatic dendritic branching defects in Drosophila class IV da neurons at late third larval instar compared with the UAS-DsRed control.
source: Expression of UAS-(GGGGCC)48 resulted in dramatic dendritic branching defects compared with the UAS-DsRed control at late third larval instar (compare Figure 4B to 4A, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from morphological analysis of Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4B, 4A, and supplementary figures.

claim: At early third instar, neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA appear nearly normal.
source: At early third instar, neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA appeared nearly normal (compare Figure 4D with 4C), with a dendrite intersection distribution similar to UAS-DsRed control neurons (compare yellow bars in Figure 4J and 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from morphological analysis of Drosophila da neurons at early third instar, with reference to Figure 4D, 4C, 4J, 4I, and supplementary figures.

claim: By late stage, dendrites in animals expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA fail to extend far from the cell body.
source: By the late stage, however, dendrites in animals expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA had failed to extend far from the cell body (compare pink bars in boxed areas in Figure 4I–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and there was a 42% decrease of distal intersections (140–360 μm from cell body) compared to early stage neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA, coinciding with a 53% loss of higher order branches (orders 13–24) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from morphological analysis of Drosophila da neurons at late third instar, with reference to Figure 4I-J and supplementary figures.

claim: There is a 42% decrease of distal intersections (140–360 μm from cell body) in late stage compared to early stage neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA.
source: By the late stage, however, dendrites in animals expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA had failed to extend far from the cell body (compare pink bars in boxed areas in Figure 4I–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and there was a 42% decrease of distal intersections (140–360 μm from cell body) compared to early stage neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA, coinciding with a 53% loss of higher order branches (orders 13–24) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from morphological analysis of Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4I-J and supplementary figures.

claim: There is a 53% loss of higher order branches (orders 13–24) in late stage compared to early stage neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA.
source: By the late stage, however, dendrites in animals expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA had failed to extend far from the cell body (compare pink bars in boxed areas in Figure 4I–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and there was a 42% decrease of distal intersections (140–360 μm from cell body) compared to early stage neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA, coinciding with a 53% loss of higher order branches (orders 13–24) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from morphological analysis of Drosophila da neurons, with reference to supplementary Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA are capable of establishing a complex dendritic arbor but subsequently fail to extend and undergo late-stage degeneration of pre-established branches.
source: These data indicated that neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA were capable of establishing a complex dendritic arbor; however, they subsequently failed to extend and underwent late-stage degeneration of pre-established branches.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of early and late stage morphology of neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 RNA.

claim: RNA binding proteins as a general class are overrepresented among mRNAs upregulated in brain samples from C9orf72 patients.
source: Both RNA binding proteins as a general class and mRNA binding proteins, more specifically, were overrepresented among mRNAs in samples from the diseased brains (Table 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data from C9orf72 patient brain samples, with reference to Table 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: mRNA binding proteins are overrepresented among mRNAs upregulated in brain samples from C9orf72 patients.
source: Both RNA binding proteins as a general class and mRNA binding proteins, more specifically, were overrepresented among mRNAs in samples from the diseased brains (Table 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data from C9orf72 patient brain samples, with reference to Table 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Downregulation of dFMR1 dramatically mitigates the UAS-(GGGGCC)48-induced dendritic branching defects.
source: These studies showed that downregulation of dFMR1 dramatically mitigated the UAS-(GGGGCC)48-induced dendritic branching defects (compare Figure 4G with 4B) with a near doubling (96% increase) of distal intersections (140–360 μm from cell body; Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic modifier analysis in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4G, 4B, and 4K.

claim: Downregulation of dFMR1 results in a 96% increase of distal intersections (140–360 μm from cell body) in neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48.
source: These studies showed that downregulation of dFMR1 dramatically mitigated the UAS-(GGGGCC)48-induced dendritic branching defects (compare Figure 4G with 4B) with a near doubling (96% increase) of distal intersections (140–360 μm from cell body; Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from genetic modifier analysis in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4K.

claim: Upregulation of dFMR1 in the context of UAS-(GGGGCC)48 expression potentiates the branching defects, reducing intersections by 70% (120–360 μm from cell body).
source: In contrast, upregulation of dFMR1 in the context of UAS-(GGGGCC)48 expression potentiated the branching defects, reducing intersections by 70% (120–360 μm from cell body; Figure 4K, compare Figure 4E with 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from genetic modifier analysis in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4K, 4E, and 4B.

claim: Downregulation of orb2 results in a 103% increase of distal intersections (140–380 μm from cell body) in neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48.
source: Studies on a second transport granule component that regulates the local translation of neuritic RNAs, Orb2 (Cziko et al., 2009; Mastushita-Sakai et al., 2010; La Via et al., 2013), showed a similar dramatic modulation of the UAS-(GGGGCC)48-induced branching defects: distal intersections were doubled upon downregulation (103% increase 140–380 μm from cell body), while upregulation resulted in a 34% overall loss (Figure 4L, compare Figure 4F and H with 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from genetic modifier analysis in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4L, 4F, 4H, and 4B, and citations to previous work on Orb2.

claim: Upregulation of orb2 in the context of UAS-(GGGGCC)48 expression results in a 34% overall loss of intersections.
source: Studies on a second transport granule component that regulates the local translation of neuritic RNAs, Orb2 (Cziko et al., 2009; Mastushita-Sakai et al., 2010; La Via et al., 2013), showed a similar dramatic modulation of the UAS-(GGGGCC)48-induced branching defects: distal intersections were doubled upon downregulation (103% increase 140–380 μm from cell body), while upregulation resulted in a 34% overall loss (Figure 4L, compare Figure 4F and H with 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from genetic modifier analysis in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4L, 4F, 4H, and 4B, and citations to previous work on Orb2.

claim: Downregulation of dFMR1 restores the number of distal intersections (140–400 μm from cell body) to 91% of late stage control in neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48.
source: Downregulation of either modifier restored the number of distal intersections (140–400 μm from cell body) compared to the late stage control, to 91% (dFMR1 RNAi), and to 94% (orb2 RNAi) (compare Figure 4G and H to A; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from genetic modifier analysis in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4G, 4H, 4A, and supplementary figures.

claim: Downregulation of orb2 restores the number of distal intersections (140–400 μm from cell body) to 94% of late stage control in neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48.
source: Downregulation of either modifier restored the number of distal intersections (140–400 μm from cell body) compared to the late stage control, to 91% (dFMR1 RNAi), and to 94% (orb2 RNAi) (compare Figure 4G and H to A; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from genetic modifier analysis in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4G, 4H, 4A, and supplementary figures.

claim: Upregulation of dFMR1 alone does not reduce the number of intersections in the absence of UAS-(GGGGCC)48.
source: Our control experiments indicated that in the absence of UAS-(GGGGCC)48, up- or downregulation of dFMR1 and orb2 resulted in minimal changes in the dendrite intersection distribution. Upregulation of dFMR1 or orb2 alone did not reduce the number of intersections (Figure 4M-N, Q-R).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from control experiments in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4M-N, Q-R.

claim: Upregulation of orb2 alone does not reduce the number of intersections in the absence of UAS-(GGGGCC)48.
source: Our control experiments indicated that in the absence of UAS-(GGGGCC)48, up- or downregulation of dFMR1 and orb2 resulted in minimal changes in the dendrite intersection distribution. Upregulation of dFMR1 or orb2 alone did not reduce the number of intersections (Figure 4M-N, Q-R).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from control experiments in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4M-N, Q-R.

claim: Knockdown of dFMR1 alone results in a 3.8% increase in distal dendrite intersections (140–400 μm from the cell body).
source: Knockdown of either dFMR1 or orb2 alone resulted in a 3.8 and 6.5% increase in distal dendrite intersections (140–400 μm from the cell body), respectively (Figure 4O-P, S-T).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from control experiments in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4O-P, S-T.

claim: Knockdown of orb2 alone results in a 6.5% increase in distal dendrite intersections (140–400 μm from the cell body).
source: Knockdown of either dFMR1 or orb2 alone resulted in a 3.8 and 6.5% increase in distal dendrite intersections (140–400 μm from the cell body), respectively (Figure 4O-P, S-T).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from control experiments in Drosophila da neurons, with reference to Figure 4O-P, S-T.

claim: Expanded GGGGCC microsatellite repeat RNA is present and transported in neurites.
source: Taken together, our data show that expanded GGGGCC microsatellite repeat RNA is present and transported in neurites, and that modulation of levels of transport granule components impacts the neuritic defects induced by the expanded microsatellite repeat RNA in vivo in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from multiple experiments showing GGGGCC RNA localization and transport in neurites.

claim: Modulation of levels of transport granule components impacts the neuritic defects induced by the expanded microsatellite repeat RNA in vivo in Drosophila.
source: Taken together, our data show that expanded GGGGCC microsatellite repeat RNA is present and transported in neurites, and that modulation of levels of transport granule components impacts the neuritic defects induced by the expanded microsatellite repeat RNA in vivo in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from genetic modifier experiments in Drosophila showing that dFMR1 and orb2 modulate GGGGCC-induced defects.

claim: Both endogenous and exogenous FMRP colocalize in neuritic granules with (GGGGCC)48-MS2 repeat RNA in neuronal processes.
source: In rat spinal cord neurons, both endogenous and exogenous FMRP colocalized in neuritic granules with (GGGGCC)48-MS2 and (CAG)100-MS2 repeat RNAs in neuronal processes (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization analysis in rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 5A-C and supplementary figures.

claim: Both endogenous and exogenous FMRP colocalize in neuritic granules with (CAG)100-MS2 repeat RNA in neuronal processes.
source: In rat spinal cord neurons, both endogenous and exogenous FMRP colocalized in neuritic granules with (GGGGCC)48-MS2 and (CAG)100-MS2 repeat RNAs in neuronal processes (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization analysis in rat spinal cord neurons, with reference to Figure 5A-C and supplementary figures.

claim: Association with FMRP is a property of multiple expanded repeat RNAs.
source: Thus, association with FMRP was a property of multiple expanded repeat RNAs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that both GGGGCC and CAG repeat RNAs colocalize with FMRP.

claim: FMRP, FXR1, and FXR2 interact with GGGGCC RNA repeats.
source: Consistent with this observation, both FMRP as well as its interaction partners FXR1 and FXR2, have been shown to interact with GGGGCC RNA repeats by assays that include pull down and proteome arrays (Almeida et al., 2013; Donnelly et al., 2013; Haeusler et al., 2014; Rossi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Almeida et al., 2013; Donnelly et al., 2013; Haeusler et al., 2014; Rossi et al., 2015).

claim: There is no evidence of altered transcript levels of FMRP target genes in cortical samples from C9orf72 patients.
source: However, we found no evidence of altered transcript levels of FMRP target genes (Darnell et al., 2011) in cortical samples from C9orf72 patients (Donnelly et al., 2013) (Table 2 and Supplementary file 1), which is consistent with a role for FMRP in post-transcriptional gene regulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of gene expression data from C9orf72 patient cortical samples, with reference to Table 2, Supplementary file 1, and citations to previous publications.

claim: The lack of altered FMRP target transcript levels is consistent with a role for FMRP in post-transcriptional gene regulation.
source: However, we found no evidence of altered transcript levels of FMRP target genes (Darnell et al., 2011) in cortical samples from C9orf72 patients (Donnelly et al., 2013) (Table 2 and Supplementary file 1), which is consistent with a role for FMRP in post-transcriptional gene regulation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that FMRP target transcript levels are not altered, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation.

claim: There is an 89–123% increase in the number of PSD-95 foci per neuron in iPSNs derived from GGGGCC repeat expansion carriers compared to controls.
source: We found an 89–123% increase in the number, but not the size, of PSD-95 foci per neuron in iPSNs derived from GGGGCC repeat expansion carriers compared to controls (Figure 5D-E,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from immunostaining analysis of iPSNs, with reference to Figure 5D-E, J.

claim: There is a 50–76% increase in total PSD-95 levels in iPSNs derived from GGGGCC repeat expansion carriers compared to controls.
source: We also saw a 50–76% increase in total PSD-95 levels (Figure 5D-E,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from immunostaining analysis of iPSNs, with reference to Figure 5D-E, K.

claim: A change in PSD-95 neuritic puncta was not seen when scoring exclusively neuritic PSD-95.
source: These results contrast with those obtained when scoring exclusively neuritic PSD-95, for which a change in PSD-95 neuritic puncta was not seen (Almeida et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Almeida et al., 2013) that analyzed neuritic PSD-95 specifically.

claim: There is a 51–130% increase in FMRP in patient-derived iPSNs compared with controls.
source: We also examined the protein levels of FMRP (which is subject to self-regulation at the mRNA level [Ashley et al., 1993]), and found a 51–130% increase in FMRP in patient-derived iPSNs compared with controls (Figure 5F-G,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from immunostaining analysis of iPSNs, with reference to Figure 5F-G, K, and citation to previous work on FMRP self-regulation.

claim: Regulation of FMRP targets could be aberrant in iPSNs derived from C9orf72 GGGGCC repeat expansion carriers.
source: These results suggest that regulation of FMRP targets could be aberrant in iPSNs derived from C9orf72 GGGGCC repeat expansion carriers.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed increases in PSD-95 and FMRP levels in carrier iPSNs.

claim: GGGGCC repeat RNA could disrupt FMRP-mediated translational repression.
source: GGGGCC repeat RNA could disrupt FMRP-mediated translational repression or increase FMRP-mRNA target stability, the latter scenario being less likely because PSD-95 mRNA levels are similar in carrier vs. control iPSNs (Almeida et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible mechanism for the observed increase in PSD-95 protein levels, with citation to previous work on PSD-95 mRNA levels.

claim: GGGGCC repeat RNA could increase FMRP-mRNA target stability, but this is less likely because PSD-95 mRNA levels are similar in carrier vs. control iPSNs.
source: GGGGCC repeat RNA could disrupt FMRP-mediated translational repression or increase FMRP-mRNA target stability, the latter scenario being less likely because PSD-95 mRNA levels are similar in carrier vs. control iPSNs (Almeida et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible but less likely mechanism, with citation to previous work on PSD-95 mRNA levels.

claim: In FMRP knockout mice, PSD-95 mRNA is destabilized and PSD-95 levels are reduced.
source: In FMRP knockout mice, PSD-95 mRNA is destabilized and PSD-95 levels reduced (Zalfa et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2011)—similarly, knockdown of FMRP might lead to destabilization of its mRNA targets, thus counteracting translational derepression by toxic GGGGCC repeat RNA in disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Zalfa et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2011).

claim: Knockdown of FMRP might lead to destabilization of its mRNA targets, thus counteracting translational derepression by toxic GGGGCC repeat RNA in disease.
source: In FMRP knockout mice, PSD-95 mRNA is destabilized and PSD-95 levels reduced (Zalfa et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2011)—similarly, knockdown of FMRP might lead to destabilization of its mRNA targets, thus counteracting translational derepression by toxic GGGGCC repeat RNA in disease.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible mechanism for how FMRP knockdown might suppress GGGGCC toxicity, based on inference from FMRP knockout mouse data.

claim: CPEB3 is a homolog of Drosophila Orb2.
source: We also analyzed a second transport granule component and local translation regulator, human CPEB3 (Huang et al., 2006; Darnell and Richter, 2012). CPEB3 is a homolog of Drosophila Orb2 that modulates GGGGCC repeat toxicity in flies (see Figure 4), and is also present in FMRP granules (Ferrari et al., 2007) and postsynaptic densities (Huang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations to previous publications.

claim: CPEB3 is present in FMRP granules.
source: We also analyzed a second transport granule component and local translation regulator, human CPEB3 (Huang et al., 2006; Darnell and Richter, 2012). CPEB3 is a homolog of Drosophila Orb2 that modulates GGGGCC repeat toxicity in flies (see Figure 4), and is also present in FMRP granules (Ferrari et al., 2007) and postsynaptic densities (Huang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Ferrari et al., 2007).

claim: CPEB3 is present in postsynaptic densities.
source: We also analyzed a second transport granule component and local translation regulator, human CPEB3 (Huang et al., 2006; Darnell and Richter, 2012). CPEB3 is a homolog of Drosophila Orb2 that modulates GGGGCC repeat toxicity in flies (see Figure 4), and is also present in FMRP granules (Ferrari et al., 2007) and postsynaptic densities (Huang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Huang et al., 2006).

claim: Total CPEB3 levels are elevated 59–118% in iPSNs with a GGGGCC repeat expansion compared to controls.
source: Total CPEB3 levels were elevated 59–118% in iPSNs with a GGGGCC repeat expansion compared to controls (Figure 5H-I,K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from immunostaining analysis of iPSNs, with reference to Figure 5H-I, K.

claim: The upregulation of CPEB3 correlates with a 60–89% increase in CPEB3 foci per neuron in carriers versus controls.
source: The upregulation correlated with a 60–89% increase in CPEB3 foci per neuron in carriers versus controls; foci size was not affected (Figure 5H-I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from immunostaining analysis of iPSNs, with reference to Figure 5H-I, J.

claim: The change in CPEB3 could be an independent effect of the toxic RNA or could be a consequence of FMRP-induced changes.
source: The change in CPEB3 could be an independent effect of the toxic RNA or could be a consequence of FMRP-induced changes.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering two possible explanations for the observed CPEB3 upregulation.

claim: There is no FMRP enrichment in the nuclei in carrier iPSNs.
source: Because we found no FMRP enrichment in the nuclei in carrier iPSNs (Figure 5L), our data do not support a nuclear GGGGCC repeat RNA-mediated FMRP sequestration model.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from immunostaining analysis of iPSNs, with reference to Figure 5L.

claim: The data do not support a nuclear GGGGCC repeat RNA-mediated FMRP sequestration model.
source: Because we found no FMRP enrichment in the nuclei in carrier iPSNs (Figure 5L), our data do not support a nuclear GGGGCC repeat RNA-mediated FMRP sequestration model.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of nuclear FMRP enrichment in carrier iPSNs.

claim: CPEB3 can modulate expression of targets of the transcription factor STAT5B.
source: CPEB3 can modulate expression of targets of the transcription factor STAT5B (Peng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Peng et al., 2010).

claim: Cortical samples from C9orf72 patients exhibit misregulation of STAT5B target genes.
source: Consistent with disruptions in CPEB3/STAT5B-modulated transcription, cortical samples from C9orf72 patients (Donnelly et al., 2013) exhibit misregulation of STAT5B target genes (Kanai et al., 2014) (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of gene expression data from C9orf72 patient cortical samples, with reference to Table 2 and citations to previous publications.

claim: Expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA may interfere with the local translation machinery and indirectly modify transcriptional programs.
source: These results indicate that expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA may interfere with the local translation machinery and indirectly modify transcriptional programs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed dysregulation of CPEB3 and STAT5B target genes.

claim: Expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs like GGGGCC that are incorporated into granules within neurites may have local effects that contribute to neurodegeneration.
source: Together, these data suggest that expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs like GGGGCC that are incorporated into granules within neurites may have local effects that contribute to neurodegeneration.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the collective experimental findings showing neuritic localization, transport, and associated defects.

claim: Expanded repeat RNAs with specific structural context can be recognized by the mRNA localization machinery.
source: Our data indicate that expanded repeat RNAs with specific structural context (e.g. stem-loop for CAG, CUG, and CCUG, and G-quadruplex and stem-loop for GGGGCC repeat RNA) can be recognized by the mRNA localization machinery, can become incorporated into neuritic RNA transport granules, and, at least for expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat RNA, may disrupt RNA granule function.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on the experimental findings showing neuritic localization of structured repeat RNAs.

claim: Expanded repeat RNAs with specific structural context can become incorporated into neuritic RNA transport granules.
source: Our data indicate that expanded repeat RNAs with specific structural context (e.g. stem-loop for CAG, CUG, and CCUG, and G-quadruplex and stem-loop for GGGGCC repeat RNA) can be recognized by the mRNA localization machinery, can become incorporated into neuritic RNA transport granules, and, at least for expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat RNA, may disrupt RNA granule function.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on the experimental findings showing neuritic localization and colocalization with transport granule components.

claim: Expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat RNA may disrupt RNA granule function.
source: Our data indicate that expanded repeat RNAs with specific structural context (e.g. stem-loop for CAG, CUG, and CCUG, and G-quadruplex and stem-loop for GGGGCC repeat RNA) can be recognized by the mRNA localization machinery, can become incorporated into neuritic RNA transport granules, and, at least for expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat RNA, may disrupt RNA granule function.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental findings showing branching defects, colocalization with FMRP, and dysregulation of transport granule components.

claim: The GGGGCC repeat can localize to the cytoplasm in disease.
source: In the case of the hexanucleotide expansion in C9orf72, although the repeat is defined as intronic, we saw neuritic GGGGCC RNA granule localization in iPSNs, indicating the repeat can localize to the cytoplasm in disease.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of neuritic GGGGCC RNA in iPSNs from expansion carriers.

claim: Among mRNAs that are localized, RNAs with stem-loop structure commonly function as cis-acting localization signals.
source: Notably among the large portion of mRNAs that are localized, RNAs with stem-loop structure commonly function as cis-acting localization signals (Ferrandon et al., 1994; Serano and Cohen, 1995; Cohen et al., 2005; Snee et al., 2005; Van De Bor et al., 2005; Dienstbier et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Ferrandon et al., 1994; Serano and Cohen, 1995; Cohen et al., 2005; Snee et al., 2005; Van De Bor et al., 2005; Dienstbier et al., 2009).

claim: In flies, 7 transcripts have been demonstrated to localize through minus-end directed transport along microtubules, and these mRNAs all contain one or more stem-loops within their localization signal.
source: Indeed, in flies, 7 transcripts have been demonstrated to localize through minus-end directed transport along microtubules, and these mRNAs all contain one or more stem-loops within their localization signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about mRNA localization in Drosophila.

claim: All mRNA localization signals with stem-loops in flies are recognized by the same localization machinery.
source: Although not similar to each other at the primary sequence level, all of these localization signals are recognized by the same localization machinery (Dienstbier et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Dienstbier et al., 2009).

claim: G-quadruplex consensus RNA sequences are cis-acting elements that are both necessary and sufficient for neuritic localization of PSD-95 and CaMKIIα.
source: In addition, G-quadruplex consensus RNA sequences have also been shown to be cis-acting elements that are both necessary and sufficient for neuritic localization of PSD-95 and CaMKIIα, two dendritically localized mRNAs (Subramanian et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Subramanian et al., 2011).

claim: About one-third of the best characterized dendritic mRNAs contain a putative G-quadruplex in their 3'UTRs.
source: Indeed, about one-third of the best characterized dendritic mRNAs contain a putative G-quadruplex in their 3'UTRs (Subramanian et al., 2011; Stefanovic et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Subramanian et al., 2011; Stefanovic et al., 2015).

claim: Neuritic localization of the expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat RNA occurs in association with neuritic defects.
source: We find that neuritic localization of the expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat RNA occurs in association with neuritic defects.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings showing correlation between neuritic GGGGCC RNA and branching defects.

claim: Neurons with expanded GGGGCC RNA granules in neurites have a decrease in primary branches compared with controls.
source: Neurons with expanded GGGGCC RNA granules in neurites have a decrease in primary branches compared with controls.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from morphological analysis of transfected rat spinal cord neurons.

claim: A comparable decrease in primary branches is not seen when the expanded RNA is localized merely to the soma.
source: We do not see a comparable decrease when the expanded RNA is localized merely to the soma, or when it is present in nuclear foci, consistent with a recent report (Tran et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from morphological analysis and citation to a recent publication (Tran et al., 2015).

claim: A comparable decrease in primary branches is not seen when the expanded RNA is present in nuclear foci.
source: We do not see a comparable decrease when the expanded RNA is localized merely to the soma, or when it is present in nuclear foci, consistent with a recent report (Tran et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from morphological analysis and citation to a recent publication (Tran et al., 2015).

claim: The branching defects associated with the neuritically localized expanded repeat are not seen with a similarly localized non-expanded (GGGGCC)3 repeat.
source: Importantly, the branching defects associated with the neuritically localized expanded repeat are not seen with a similarly localized non-expanded (GGGGCC)3 repeat—branching in neurons with neuritic non-expanded repeat is not significantly different from branching in neurons with somatic or nuclear expanded repeat.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from morphological analysis comparing (GGGGCC)48-MS2 and (GGGGCC)3-MS2.

claim: The incorporation of expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs into granules within neurites induces dysfunction.
source: These data indicate that the incorporation of expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs into granules within neurites induces dysfunction.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental findings showing branching defects associated with neuritic expanded repeat RNA.

claim: In vivo, the dendritic arbors of da neurons expressing UAS-(GGGGCC)48 are normal early, but later show a different pattern with fewer intersections and smaller field.
source: In vivo, the dendritic arbors of da neurons are normal early, but later show a different pattern with fewer intersections and smaller field.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from morphological analysis of Drosophila da neurons at different developmental stages.

claim: The effect of UAS-(GGGGCC)48 on da neuron morphology is distinct from defects in endosomal transport, as described for dynein loss-of-function mutations.
source: This effect is distinct from defects in endosomal transport, as described for dynein loss-of-function mutations (Satoh et al., 2008), indicating it is unlikely to be due to vesicular traffic transport defects.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison with known dynein loss-of-function phenotypes, with citation to a previous publication (Satoh et al., 2008).

claim: dFMR1 and Orb2 are novel modifiers of GGGGCC toxicity.
source: Furthermore, two transport granule components (FMRP and Orb2, the fly CPEB3 ortholog) are novel modifiers of GGGGCC toxicity.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from genetic modifier analysis in Drosophila.

claim: The FMRP target PSD-95 appears present at elevated levels in iPSNs from C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion carriers.
source: Our studies also provide evidence that the expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA may compromise local translation regulation: the FMRP targets, PSD-95 and FMRP, appeared present at elevated levels in iPSNs from C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion carriers.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining analysis of iPSNs.

claim: FMRP appears present at elevated levels in iPSNs from C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion carriers.
source: Our studies also provide evidence that the expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA may compromise local translation regulation: the FMRP targets, PSD-95 and FMRP, appeared present at elevated levels in iPSNs from C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion carriers.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining analysis of iPSNs.

claim: PSD-95 mRNA levels are similar in carrier vs. control iPSNs.
source: GGGGCC repeat RNA could disrupt FMRP-mediated translational repression or increase FMRP-mRNA target stability, the latter scenario being less likely because PSD-95 mRNA levels are similar in carrier vs. control iPSNs (Almeida et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Almeida et al., 2013).

claim: Knockdown of FMRP might counteract translational derepression by toxic GGGGCC repeat RNA in disease by destabilizing FMRP mRNA targets.
source: In FMRP knockout mice, PSD-95 mRNA is destabilized and PSD-95 levels reduced (Zalfa et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2011)—similarly, knockdown of FMRP might lead to destabilization of its mRNA targets, thus counteracting translational derepression by toxic GGGGCC repeat RNA in disease.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible mechanism for how FMRP knockdown might suppress GGGGCC toxicity, based on inference from FMRP knockout mouse data.

claim: CPEB3/STAT5B-regulated genes are dysregulated in samples from C9orf72 patient cortex.
source: Consistent with our observation that CPEB3 protein levels are upregulated in iPSNs from GGGGCC expansion carriers, we find CPEB3/STAT5B-regulated genes are dysregulated in samples from C9orf72 patient cortex (Donnelly et al., 2013), see Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of gene expression data from C9orf72 patient cortical samples, with reference to Table 2 and citation to a previous publication.

claim: RAN translation products generated from the GGGGCC repeat RNA can be toxic.
source: A study in the fly showed that RAN translation products generated from the GGGGCC repeat RNA can be toxic.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a previous study in flies.

claim: A GGGGCC repeat is toxic in vivo, but toxicity is minimal if the sequence is interrupted by stop codons.
source: Moreover, they found that a GGGGCC repeat is toxic in vivo, but toxicity is minimal if the sequence is not a pure GGGGCC, but is interrupted by stop codons (and thus could not code for peptides) (Mizielinska et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous publication (Mizielinska et al., 2014).

claim: Alterations in the RNA sequence required to block RAN translation may interfere with RNA-protein interactions required for subcellular RNA localization and/or toxicity.
source: However, alterations in the RNA sequence required to block RAN translation (introduction of stop codons) may well interfere with the intricacy of RNA-protein interactions, such as those required for subcellular RNA localization, and/or those that mediate toxicity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible explanation for why stop codon interruption reduces toxicity.

claim: Mechanisms beyond RAN translation may contribute to neurodegeneration conferred by expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA.
source: Mechanisms beyond RAN translation may well contribute to neurodegeneration conferred by expanded GGGGCC repeat RNA.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental findings showing RNA-mediated effects independent of detectable RAN translation.

claim: Targeting of expanded microsatellite repeat RNA to neuritic granules may disrupt local mRNA translation.
source: Targeting of expanded microsatellite repeat RNA to the neuritic granules that we document may disrupt local mRNA translation, and might also interfere with proper trafficking of cellular RNAs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible mechanism for how neuritic repeat RNA causes toxicity.

claim: Targeting of expanded microsatellite repeat RNA to neuritic granules might interfere with proper trafficking of cellular RNAs.
source: Targeting of expanded microsatellite repeat RNA to the neuritic granules that we document may disrupt local mRNA translation, and might also interfere with proper trafficking of cellular RNAs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible mechanism for how neuritic repeat RNA causes toxicity.

claim: The presence of microsatellite repeat RNA in neurites might result in local RAN translation.
source: We speculate that the presence of microsatellite repeat RNA in neurites might also result in local RAN translation, and that RAN translation products in the neuritic subcellular compartment could contribute to neurite loss.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible mechanism for how neuritic repeat RNA causes toxicity.

claim: RAN translation products in the neuritic subcellular compartment could contribute to neurite loss.
source: We speculate that the presence of microsatellite repeat RNA in neurites might also result in local RAN translation, and that RAN translation products in the neuritic subcellular compartment could contribute to neurite loss.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible mechanism for how neuritic repeat RNA causes toxicity.

claim: Neuritically localized expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs associate with neuritic RNP granule components and disrupt their function, resulting in neuritic defects.
source: Our data support a novel model in which neuritically localized expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs associate with neuritic RNP granule components and disrupt their function, resulting in neuritic defects.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: This mechanism may contribute to ALS/FTD disease in patients bearing the GGGGCC repeat expansion.
source: This mechanism may contribute to ALS/FTD disease in patients bearing the GGGGCC repeat expansion, as we have shown strong effects in iPSC-derived neurons from GGGGCC expansion carriers, in cultured rat spinal cord neurons, and in vivo in a Drosophila model.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental findings across multiple model systems.

claim: Many different expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs are incorporated into neuritic granules in culture.
source: In culture, we have shown many different expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs are incorporated into neuritic granules, and at least several are actively transported.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings showing neuritic localization of CAG, CUG, CCUG, and GGGGCC repeat RNAs.

claim: At least several expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs are actively transported in neurites.
source: In culture, we have shown many different expanded microsatellite repeat RNAs are incorporated into neuritic granules, and at least several are actively transported.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from time-lapse imaging showing transport of GGGGCC and CAG repeat RNAs.

claim: hnRNP A3 is implicated in transport granule function.
source: For the GGGGCC repeat, a number of proteins that bind the repeat (hnRNP A3) or are modifiers of GGGGCC repeat toxicity (Pur alpha and hnRNP A2/B1) are implicated in transport granule function (Jin et al., 2007; Sofola et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Jin et al., 2007; Sofola et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: Mutations in TDP-43 impair neuritic mRNA transport in primary and stem-cell derived neurons.
source: Interestingly, mutations in TDP-43 impair neuritic mRNA transport in primary and stem-cell derived neurons and are causative of ALS (Alami et al., 2014); TDP-43 pathology also characterizes many repeat expansion diseases (Elden et al., 2010; Toyoshima and Takahashi, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications (Alami et al., 2014).
